Luciano Pavarotti. An Italian tenor whose extraordinary voice and charismatic stage presence made him the most famous opera singer of the late twentieth century. Born in Modena, he dominated the tenor repertoire from the nineteen-sixties onward and brought opera to global popular audiences through recordings, television, and crossover performances. His signature role, Calaf in Puccini's Turandot, and his definitive recording of Nessun dorma remain defining moments in operatic recording history.

Pavarotti made his professional debut in nineteen sixty-one and rose to prominence through the nineteen-sixties and seventies at La Scala Milan and other major houses. He possessed an exceptionally bright, easily soaring spinto tenor voice with uncommon staying power and projection.

Nessun dorma, which means None Shall Sleep, from Turandot became his signature aria. His nineteen seventy-two recording defined the role for modern audiences. Pavarotti was known for his gift for promotion. He used television and recordings to build a mass audience for opera at a time it was declining.

He collaborated frequently with conductor Herbert von Karajan and soprano Joan Sutherland, creating legendary performances together. Pavarotti performed the role of Rodolfo in La Bohème over one thousand times throughout his career, making it second nature. He was a cultural ambassador who brought opera singers into collaboration with pop musicians and performed at major international events.

The tenor is his voice type, the heroic protagonist voice in opera. Nessun dorma is his greatest signature aria, inextricably linked to his legacy. Turandot is the Puccini opera containing his defining role. Opera is his entire artistic career and life context. Puccini is the composer whose works, especially Turandot and La Bohème, defined Pavarotti's repertoire.
